title: Data structures
theory: Choose a representation based on the operations you need: insertion, removal, lookup, traversal, and ordering. The representation imposes trade-offs rather than being universally best.
A linked-list node contains data and a link. Inserting or removing a node changes links as well as ownership. Save the next address before freeing the current node while traversing a list.

A stack removes the most recently added item. A queue removes the earliest added item. Specify empty behavior explicitly. A hash table uses a hash to select a bucket and still needs collision handling.

The local tests check the observable contract, including empty and repeated cases. They do not prove that you used a linked list or achieved a complexity bound. Record your representation and review it against the rubric.

quiz.prompt: Push 2, then 7, then pop a stack. Result?
Two keys hash to the same bucket. This is?
quiz.explanation: Different keys can map to the same bucket.

quiz.prompt: Before freeing the current linked-list node during traversal, save what?
quiz.explanation: Reading current->next after freeing current would access freed storage.

quiz.prompt: Which is generally a drawback of a singly linked list compared with an array?
options: No direct constant-time indexing by position
quiz.explanation: Reaching a position usually requires following links.

quiz.prompt: A data structure should be chosen mainly by?
quiz.explanation: The workload determines which trade-offs are useful.
